newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese start voting in poll for 21st century.
newsitem.headline: Japanese start voting in poll for 21st century.

text.p: Japanese started voting on Sunday in the first general election for three years with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto hoping for a big turnout to help his Liberal Democratic Party win back sole power.
"The voting turnout will be a key factor," NHK television said in its first report on election day.
A record 1,503 candidates from nine parties are contesting the poll, the first to be held under a new electoral system meant to foster party politics and issues instead of individual pork barrelling.
Political leaders have described the poll as a "landmark" and "turning point" because it will elect a government for the next four years to lead Japan into the 21st century.
Under the new system, the Lower House is reduced to 500 seats from 511 and multi-seat constituencies are abolished.
Voters elect 300 single-seat candidates, while 200 seats are decided by proportional representation.

The election is being held nearly one year ahead of schedule because of Hashimoto's belief that at this time he can win sole power for his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and end three years of coalition rule.
There were few signs of queues when the polls opened at 7 a.m. (2200 GMT, Saturday) with overcast but fine weather forecast for most of the nation.
Voting ends at 6 p.m. (0900 GMT) and first official results are expected about an hour later with counting ending and a likely result declared about 2 a.m. on Monday (1700 GMT, Sunday).

Polls forecast a possible majority by the LDP which led a coalition of the Socialists and the Sakigake Party, an LDP splinter group, in the last parliament. Hashimoto has been prime minister since last January.
In the main policy difference, the opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) opposes an LDP plan to raise the sales tax from three to five per cent from April and instead proposes income tax cuts.

Analysts warn the outcome is unpredictable because of surveys which show there could be a record low turnout because of voter dissatisfaction with politics in general and few differences between the major parties.
"Please come and vote," Hashimoto told Tokyo rallies on the eve of the election.
The surveys show turnout may be below 60 percent, worse than the post-war record low of 67.26 percent in the last election in 1993.

If the poll forecasts of an LDP win hold up, it would be a remarkable comeback by the party, which has steadily built itself up since 1993, when it lost power for the first time in 38 years because of a series of financial scandals.
It clawed its way into a coalition government one year after the setback, but with only 211 seats in the previous parliament, it had to share power with the two smaller parties.
In the old house, Shinshinto held 160 seats.
The balance of power could be decided by the fledgling Democratic Party, formed only last month with 52 Lower House defectors from the Socialists and Sakigake.
